outcome: Since 26 January 2024 a counterexample has been claimed: OpenAI's preprint 'A finitely generated counterexample to the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture' (first publicly visible in the openai/math GitHub repository on 6 Oct 2026; the document itself is dated 23 Sep 2026) gives a finitely generated residually finite group with integral cohomological dimension 2 and geometric dimension 3, with a Lean challenge/solution pair whose solution module my text-level scan found free of sorry; no qualified human has publicly checked the argument in any source I could read. Two earlier human preprints (Kawauchi, arXiv:2303.04368, 2023, revised 2024; Pasku, arXiv:2107.12293, 2021, v2 Oct 2026) claim Whitehead's asphericity question is answered positively, which by the Bestvina–Brady dichotomy would make the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture false; neither has any uptake in the sources read.
problem_asks: The bullet asks one universal claim, which has three parts. (1) For every group G (no restriction to finitely presented, torsion-free or countable groups). (2) If G has cohomological dimension 2: the bullet names no coefficient ring, so I read this as integral cohomological dimension cd_Z(G) = 2 (flagged as an assumption; the standard reading). (3) Then G has a 2-dimensional Eilenberg–MacLane space K(G,1): a 2-dimensional aspherical CW complex with fundamental group G, equivalently geometric dimension gd(G) = 2. The claim fails exactly when some G has cd(G) = 2 and no 2-dimensional K(G,1) (then gd(G) = 3, since gd(G) ≤ 3 is known). Not asked by this bullet, but needed as context: the cases cd(G) ≠ 2 (settled by Eilenberg–Ganea 1957 for cd ≥ 3, and by Stallings–Swan for cd = 1); and Whitehead's asphericity question, which Bestvina–Brady link to this bullet but which is a separate conjecture.

events.what_happened: Eilenberg and Ganea, 'On the Lusternik–Schnirelmann category of abstract groups', Annals of Mathematics 65 (1957) 517–518 (DOI 10.2307/1970062 as cited by Wikipedia). They showed gd(G) = cd(G) whenever cd(G) ≥ 3 and that cd(G) = 2 forces gd(G) ≤ 3. Background event, not a resolution of the bullet. The 1957 paper itself was not opened; the content is taken from the Wikipedia lead and from search-result summaries.
events.delivers: Settles the bullet for every group with cd ≠ 2 (cd ≥ 3: gd = cd). For cd = 2 it gives only gd ≤ 3. Nothing about the cd = 2 case beyond that bound.
events.remains: Every group with cd(G) = 2: whether gd(G) = 2. This is the whole bullet.

events.direction: Partial positive: consistent with the bullet for cd ≥ 3 (no counterexample there). Says nothing that cuts for or against the cd = 2 claim.

events.what_happened: Bestvina and Brady, 'Morse theory and finiteness properties of groups', Inventiones Mathematicae 129 (1997) 445–470 (DOI 10.1007/s002220050168). They construct groups B_L (height kernels of right-angled Artin groups built from finite flag complexes L) and prove that either B_L is a counterexample to the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture or there is a counterexample to Whitehead's asphericity conjecture, so both cannot be true. The date given is the best available preprint year (search-result summary of the PDF's first page showing 1995/1996 submission dates); not verified against the preprint itself. Journal year is 1997.
events.revisions: Journal version Invent. Math. 129 (1997) 445–470. Preprint year 1996 is from a search-result summary, not from the preprint.
events.delivers: A dichotomy linking the bullet to Whitehead's asphericity question: EG fails or Whitehead fails. It does not decide the bullet, and it is not a resolution of either conjecture.
events.remains: The whole bullet, and Whitehead's question.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (citation per Wikipedia; not opened)

events.time_since_posted: about 30 years (journal); about 30 years (preprint, per the 1996 year)
events.direction: Neither way: a reduction that ties the bullet to Whitehead's question. It is cited by the Wikipedia articles on both conjectures and by the 2026 Leary–Petrosyan preprint (event below).

events.what_happened: Fluch and Leary, 'An Eilenberg–Ganea phenomenon for actions with virtually cyclic stabilisers', arXiv:1207.1474 (v1 5 Jul 2012; v2 24 Apr 2014, which its arXiv comment says is 'as accepted by Groups, Geometry and Dynamics'). For some Coxeter groups and the family of virtually cyclic subgroups, they show the Bredon cohomological dimension is 2 while the Bredon geometric dimension is 3. This is a family (Bredon) variant. The classical statement is not addressed in the abstract; the construction was not read.
events.revisions: v2 24 Apr 2014, accepted by Groups, Geometry and Dynamics per the arXiv comment.
events.delivers: A counterexample to the Bredon (family) analogue of the conjecture for the family of virtually cyclic subgroups, for some Coxeter groups. Carries the family restriction: it says nothing about the classical family (trivial family), which is the bullet.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper, per the arXiv comment; journal page not opened

events.direction: Family/Bredon analogue fails; the classical question is not addressed. Discounted: a different question under the scope rule.
events.object: Coxeter groups (construction not read; abstract only) whose Bredon cohomological dimension is 2 and Bredon geometric dimension is 3 for the family of virtually cyclic subgroups.

events.what_happened: Brady, Leary and Nucinkis (2001): right-angled Coxeter groups W with cd_FIN(W) = 2 and gd_FIN(W) = 3 for the family of finite subgroups, so the family version of the conjecture fails. Known to me only through secondary sources (a thesis, Crisp's survey, and the Sánchez Saldaña 2019 paper as summarised in search results). The 2001 paper was not opened.
events.delivers: A counterexample to the family-of-finite-subgroups (Bredon-type) version only. Not the classical statement.
events.doubts: Not opened: every detail comes from secondary summaries (the nerve condition and the group family). Treat the description as unverified until the 2001 paper is read.
events.direction: Family/Bredon analogue fails; discounted under the scope rule.
events.object: Right-angled Coxeter groups whose nerve is an acyclic 2-complex that does not embed in any contractible 2-complex (per a search-result summary; not read).

events.what_happened: Gersten, 'Asphericity for certain groups of cohomological dimension 2', arXiv:1501.06875 (v1 27 Jan 2015; v2 12 Feb 2015; v3 16 Mar 2015). Abstract: a finite connected 2-complex K whose fundamental group has cohomological dimension 2 is aspherical iff the subgroup Σ_K of H_2(K) of spherical 2-cycles is zero; a finite connected subcomplex of an aspherical 2-complex is aspherical iff its fundamental group has cohomological dimension 2; a result on projective Z[G]-modules for countable G of cd 2.
events.delivers: Reformulations: a criterion for asphericity of a given finite 2-complex, and a Whitehead-type equivalence for finite subcomplexes. Per the abstract, no class of cd-2 groups is shown to have 2-dimensional models.
events.remains: The whole bullet. The criterion has to be checked complex by complex.
events.doubts: Only the abstract was read. The body may contain specific classes; none is stated in the abstract.
events.direction: A reformulation, not a cut in either direction.

events.what_happened: Pasku, 'A semigroup theoretic approach to Whitehead's asphericity question', arXiv:1407.6283. Current version v7 (22 Jan 2019) abstract: a combinatorial characterization of asphericity via the 'weak dominion' of a submonoid, and 'a sufficient and necessary condition under which a subpresentation of an aspherical group presentation is aspherical'. Version history: v1 23 Jul 2014; v2 31 Jul 2014 marked '(withdrawn)'; v3 4 Aug 2014; v4 6 Aug 2014 marked '(withdrawn)'; v5 22 Sep 2014; v6 9 Apr 2016; v7 22 Jan 2019. The listing gives no withdrawal notice text. A search-result summary reports an earlier title on the same arXiv ID, 'A proof for the Whitehead asphericity problem' (not verified: the earlier version text was not opened). Kawauchi (2023) says a Pasku preprint reports the same Whitehead result; which Pasku ID he meant is not established.
events.revisions: v2 31 Jul 2014 (withdrawn); v3 4 Aug 2014; v4 6 Aug 2014 (withdrawn); v5 22 Sep 2014; v6 9 Apr 2016; v7 22 Jan 2019 (current).
events.delivers: Per the current abstract: a characterization of subpresentation asphericity, a necessary and sufficient condition. It does not state an answer to Whitehead's question, and it does not make a claim about the bullet.
events.remains: Whether Whitehead's question is answered (positively or negatively) is not stated in the current abstract. The bullet is untouched on the abstract.
events.doubts: Two versions are marked withdrawn with no notice text. An earlier title (per a search-result summary) suggested a full proof, while the current abstract stops at a characterization. The reason for the withdrawals is not given in the listing.

withdrawn.by: not stated in the listing (author or arXiv)

events.direction: A characterization. It does not claim a counterexample, and on the current abstract it does not claim a positive answer either.

events.what_happened: Kawauchi, 'Whitehead aspherical conjecture via ribbon sphere-link', arXiv:2303.04368 (v1 8 Mar 2023; v2 9 Apr 2024). Theorem 1.1 (v2): 'Whitehead Aspherical Conjecture is true': every connected subcomplex of any aspherical 2-complex is aspherical. Method per the v2 text: reduce Conjecture 1 to Conjecture 2 (locally finite contractible 2-complexes), then to Conjecture 3 (subcomplexes of homology-trivial unit-group presentations), then build for each presentation a ribbon S²-link whose exterior has free fundamental group, and use aspherical closed exteriors of ribbon disk-links. The abstract says the finite contractible case was already confirmed by ribbon sphere-links, and v2 extends it to all aspherical 2-complexes. The paper does not mention the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture or Bestvina–Brady. The v1 text was not compared with v2.
events.revisions: v2 9 Apr 2024 (inside the window). Changes between v1 and v2 not identified.
events.delivers: Claims Whitehead's asphericity conjecture, which is a different bullet, as true. The Eilenberg–Ganea consequence is not in the paper; it follows only through the Bestvina–Brady dichotomy (which Wikipedia's Whitehead article and the Pasku preprint both state): a true Whitehead conjecture would force the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture to fail. Nothing about the bullet is shown in the paper itself.
events.remains: The bullet, as far as this paper goes (no statement about cd-2 groups is made in the paper). The implication for the bullet is by the dichotomy, not by the paper.
events.doubts: No journal publication found. No expert review found in any search. Wikipedia's Whitehead article (fetched 11 Oct 2026) lists the conjecture as an unsolved problem and does not mention this paper. A 2026 blog comment by Xiaolei Wu ('OK, at least the Whitehead Conjecture has not fallen') is consistent with Whitehead still being treated as open, but it is not an evaluation of this paper. I read the paper's outline in a summary, not its full body.
events.direction: Cuts toward Whitehead's conjecture being true (and so, via Bestvina–Brady, toward the bullet being false). The paper itself does not cut on the bullet.

events.what_happened: Martínez-Pedroza and Sánchez Saldaña, 'Bowditch Taut Spectrum and dimensions of groups', arXiv:2107.10643 (v1 22 Jul 2021; v2 15 Dec 2021). Published in Michigan Math. J. 74(3) (2024) according to a Project Euclid listing seen in search results (not opened). Abstract, read verbatim: 'We also show that if there is a finitely presented counter-example to the Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture, then there are continuously many finitely generated one-ended non-quasi-isometric counter-examples.' The abstract also lists classes of finitely generated groups (with cd and gd written in underlined notation that the extraction garbled) containing continuously many one-ended non-quasi-isometric groups, and states an 'Eilenberg-Ganea phenomenon for families'.
events.revisions: v2 15 Dec 2021. Journal publication Michigan Math. J. 74(3) (2024) per search-result listing, not opened.
events.delivers: Conditional: if a finitely presented counterexample exists, there are continuum many finitely generated one-ended non-quasi-isometric counterexamples. It does not produce a counterexample. The unconditional bullets are in a class of groups whose dimension notation I could not read reliably; they may be family versions. This is an open reading for the judging pass.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published vol. 74 issue 3 (2024) per listing; not opened

If they are classical cd and gd, they would be a much larger claim than the paper's conditional phrasing suggests; the conditional wording indicates they are not. The judging pass should read the PDF before relying on that.

events.what_happened: Sánchez Saldaña, 'Groups acting on trees and the Eilenberg–Ganea problem for families', arXiv:1911.03457 (v1 7 Nov 2019; v2 7 Oct 2020, minor corrections; arXiv comment 'Version accepted for publication in Proceedings of the AMS'). Constructs new groups with cd = 2 and gd = 3 for the families of finite subgroups, virtually abelian groups of bounded rank, and virtually poly-cyclic subgroups, using Brady–Leary–Nucinkis and Fluch–Leary examples and Bass–Serre theory. The abstract does not use the word 'counterexample' and calls them 'new examples'.

events.what_happened: Pasku, 'An answer to the Whitehead asphericity question', arXiv:2107.12293 (v1 26 Jul 2021, 41 pages per the listing; v2 5 Oct 2026, current; the v2 listing carries an admin note of text overlap with arXiv:1407.6283). Abstract: Whitehead's question (whether a subpresentation of an aspherical presentation is aspherical) is answered 'positively' by proving that if P = (x, r) is an aspherical presentation of the trivial group and r0 a fixed relation, then (x, r minus r0) is aspherical. Introduction (v2): 'An immediate implication of our result and that of Bestvina-Brady is that the conjecture of Eilenberg and Ganea is false.' The v1 text was not compared with v2, and no change log was seen.
events.revisions: v2 5 Oct 2026, one day before the OpenAI release. Changes from v1 not identified.
events.delivers: Claims a positive answer to Whitehead's question, and through Bestvina–Brady, that the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture is false. The stated theorem is narrower than the general question claimed: it covers presentations of the trivial group with one relation removed. The reduction from that case to the general question is attributed in search-result summaries to Howie (1983) and Luft (1996); I did not verify it, and the paper's abstract does not state it.
events.remains: On the paper's own claim, nothing of the bullet remains. On the narrower theorem stated in the abstract, the general Whitehead question and therefore the bullet's negative consequence are not established.
events.doubts: (a) The stated theorem covers the trivial-group, one-relation case; the general claim needs a reduction that the abstract does not state. (b) No journal publication and no expert engagement found in any search. (c) v2 appeared five years after v1 with no visible change log, one day before the OpenAI release. (d) Kawauchi (2023) says a Pasku preprint reports the same Whitehead result by a group-theoretic argument; which Pasku arXiv ID is meant, and whether the two Pasku preprints agree, is not established. (e) Wikipedia's Whitehead article (Oct 2026) does not mention this paper.
events.direction: Claims a positive answer to Whitehead's question, and thereby (via Bestvina–Brady) a counterexample to the bullet.

events.what_happened: Leary and Petrosyan, 'Universal Structure of Graph Product Kernels', arXiv:2605.07853 (submitted 8 May 2026; one version). The main subject is functorial structure of graph-product kernels. Section 5.6 states the conjecture (Conjecture 5.20: 'If a group G has cd G = 2, then there exists a 2-dimensional K(G,1)-complex'), cites the Bestvina–Brady disjunction, quotes Davis calling B_L 'a more convincing candidate for a counterexample' than [W_L,W_L], and proves Corollary 5.21: 'If [W_L,W_L] is a counterexample to the Eilenberg-Ganea Conjecture, then B_L is a counterexample as well.' The paper constructs no counterexample.
events.delivers: A conditional transfer: a counterexample of the form [W_L,W_L] would give one of the form B_L. Restricted to those two families.
events.direction: Conditional. Cuts toward the B_L family as a candidate, per the cited remark by Davis, without deciding it.

events.what_happened: Issue #1794 'Eilenberg-Ganea Conjecture' in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, opened 20 Jan 2026 by franzhusch (status Open; labels 'new conjecture' and 'needs-prerequisites'; placed in the 'Wikipedia, Algebra' milestone by mo271 on 23 Jan 2026). The issue body states the conjecture and says 'Created by AI, reviewed by me'. It records a formalizability rating of 4/5 and that Mathlib lacks prerequisites such as cohomological dimension for groups and Eilenberg–MacLane spaces. This is a formal-statement proposal, not a mathematical result.
events.delivers: Nothing about the mathematics. A formal statement of the conjecture in a benchmark repository, and a record that the needed definitions were absent from Mathlib in January 2026.

events.what_happened: OpenAI posted, in the openai/math GitHub repository, a preprint titled 'A finitely generated counterexample to the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture' (author 'OpenAI'; README, preamble and folder dated 23 Sep 2026), together with a scope note lean/docs/249.md ('A finitely generated Eilenberg–Ganea counterexample'), a Comparator challenge file lean/ComparatorChallenges/EilenbergGanea.lean and its JSON configuration, and a solution module lean/OAI/Topology/EilenbergGanea/Main.lean (theorem OAI.EilenbergGanea.source_main). The claim is that a finitely generated residually finite group G has integral cd 2 and gd 3, so it has a 3-dimensional classifying space and no 2-dimensional one. The release was announced in OpenAI's post 'Sharing AI progress in mathematics' (6 Oct 2026; the page returned HTTP 403 to my fetch). Wikipedia's Eilenberg–Ganea article (fetched 11 Oct 2026) reports the claim as made on 6 Oct 2026 and cites the 23 Sep preprint. A catalogue secondary source (kingy.ai) lists it as family 249, 'Lean scope'. The paper's introduction, read via a summary, describes G as the height kernel of a right-angled Artin group A_L, where L is a finite acyclic flag triangulation of the presentation complex of ⟨x,y | x²=y⁵, x²=(xy⁻¹)³⟩, which is a Bestvina–Brady group. The Lean file's definitions use an 'Artin group of a seed graph' with seven vertices (51 edges and 45 sectors per its docstring), and I did not reconcile the two descriptions. The Lean statement source_main is the conjunction: FG, residually finite, cohomologicalDimension = 2, HasClassifyingSpace 3, and not HasClassifyingSpace 2.
events.revisions: Authors' date 23 Sep 2026 (README, preamble, folder name). First visible public commit 6 Oct 2026, 'Initial commit' (hash adc7f12); the path's commit list showed only that commit. 7 Oct 2026: the repository withdrew three other manuscripts (a sign error broke an argument used by two papers) and revised 14 others; no change to this manuscript was found in my sources. Current revision state of this manuscript not verified.
events.delivers: A counterexample to the bullet as stated: a finitely generated residually finite group with integral cd 2 and gd 3, so no 2-dimensional K(G,1) exists for it. Restrictions: the dimension is integral cohomological dimension; the group is a Bestvina–Brady-type height kernel; the claim is about the classical (trivial family) statement. Its strength depends on the Lean definitions matching the standard notions, which is unverified (see doubts).
events.remains: Nothing of the bullet's universal claim survives if the counterexample holds. The paper addresses no other part of the bullet and does not settle Whitehead's question, which is a separate bullet. Whether the result stands is not established by any source I read.
events.time_since_posted: under one week (6 Oct to 11 Oct 2026)

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 with Mathlib, as a Comparator challenge/solution pair (lean/ComparatorChallenges/EilenbergGanea.json; permitted axioms propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice). I did not build or run it. Sorry status comes from reads of the raw files by a summarising tool. The challenge file has one sorry by design (theorem source_main, line 114 or 116 depending on read). The solution module and its direct imports have none by keyword scan. The transitive import closure was not fully checked.

events.directly_checkable: The group is given by a presentation in the paper's introduction and by the Lean definitions. The cd = 2 claim is proved in the solution modules through a finite combinatorial contraction (SeedChainCertificate). The nonexistence of a 2-dimensional model is proved in Dimension.lean via the lemma source_no_boundary_basis, which says no presentation has its relators as an integral basis of Cayley cycles. I did not check any of this by hand.
events.doubts: (1) No qualified human has publicly checked the argument in any source I could read. The public remarks are not checks. Xiaolei Wu (undated comment in a blog post updated 11 Oct 2026): 'Eilenberg-Ganea is false—not so surprising, perhaps, but how?'. Grigori Avramidi (11 Oct 2026) agrees with Ian Agol's closing remark. Ian Agol's comment (8 Oct 2026, same post) is conditional, 'assuming they get checked to be correct', and in the portion I read it does not name the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture. Kimball Martin in the same thread: 'A Lean verification does not show the written proof is correct.' (2) Formal faithfulness: the Lean statement uses the repository's own library (OAI.*) for cohomologicalDimension (projective dimension of the trivial integral module), HasClassifyingSpace (a repository-defined CW-complex notion), and ResiduallyFinite, not Mathlib. DeepMind's issue #1794 (Jan 2026) records that Mathlib then lacked cohomological dimension for groups and Eilenberg–MacLane spaces. Comparator checks a solution against the challenge statement; it does not check that these definitions match the standard notions. (3) Scale and build: the certificate modules carry large data tables (lists of Fin 372 × ℤ and Fin 270 × ℤ pairs, chunked natural-number literals), and I could not see whether kernel decide or another check is used. I found no build log and no independent Lean run; kingy.ai states 'no independent Lean execution'. (4) Date: the authors date the preprint 23 Sep 2026, the first public commit is 6 Oct 2026. (5) Release record: three manuscripts were withdrawn and fourteen revised on 7 Oct 2026, and the README says 'Some of the unformalized results could have issues.' This manuscript is formalized, but the same release has had errors. (6) Attribution: the manuscript itself (README, preamble, introduction as summarised) names no model, prompts, human role or verification method. See the ai field.
events.direction: Cuts against the bullet: asserts a group with cd 2 and no 2-dimensional K(G,1), which the bullet's universal claim forbids. Its consistency with the Bestvina–Brady dichotomy is not in question: the group is a Bestvina–Brady-type kernel, which is the family Davis and Leary–Petrosyan had named as the more convincing candidate.
events.object: A finitely generated residually finite group G: the height kernel of a right-angled Artin group (per the paper's introduction) over a finite acyclic flag triangulation L of the presentation complex of ⟨x,y | x²=y⁵, x²=(xy⁻¹)³⟩ (a Bestvina–Brady group). It shows integral cd(G) = 2 and gd(G) = 3: a 3-dimensional classifying space exists and no 2-dimensional one does. The group is explicitly presented. The nonexistence of a 2-dimensional model is proved by a homological (integral boundary-basis) argument, not exhibited, so this is a non-constructive proof of a negative statement.

disputes.summary: Kawauchi (arXiv:2303.04368, March 2023) states that a preprint by E. Pasku reports the same Whitehead result by a group-theoretic argument much different from his own. Pasku has at least two arXiv IDs on the question: 1407.6283 (2014–2019, two versions marked withdrawn) and 2107.12293 (2021; v2 Oct 2026). Which one Kawauchi meant is not established, and the two Pasku preprints have not been compared in any source I read.

summary: Forty web searches and about fifty pages were run, with the search log below. The one new claim since January 2024 that bears on the bullet directly is OpenAI's preprint 'A finitely generated counterexample to the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture' in the openai/math repository, first publicly visible on 6 Oct 2026 (the document, README and folder say 23 Sep 2026). Its introduction, read through a summary because the PDF is binary and my tools could not read it, describes a finitely generated residually finite group, the height kernel of a right-angled Artin group on a finite acyclic flag triangulation of the presentation complex of ⟨x,y | x²=y⁵, x²=(xy⁻¹)³⟩, with integral cd 2 and gd 3. The Lean challenge file states exactly this conjunction with one sorry, in theorem source_main, and the solution module OAI/Topology/EilenbergGanea/Main.lean (named in the Comparator JSON) and its direct imports show no sorry in a keyword scan of raw files read through a summarising tool. I did not compile anything (curl was blocked by the permission setting), and the transitive import closure is much larger than the roughly thirteen modules I scanned, so 'sorry-free' here means a text scan of the modules I looked at, not a build. The Lean definitions of cohomologicalDimension, HasClassifyingSpace, CW complexes and residual finiteness live in OpenAI's own library rather than Mathlib, which DeepMind's issue #1794 (Jan 2026) records as lacking cohomological dimension for groups; so the Comparator check certifies the proof against the statement as written there, and whether that matches the standard notions is unchecked. The public reactions I could read are not checks: Xiaolei Wu's 'Eilenberg-Ganea is false—not so surprising, perhaps, but how?', Grigori Avramidi's 11 Oct agreement with Ian Agol's closing remark, Agol's own conditional remark ('assuming they get checked to be correct', which does not name the conjecture in the portion I read), and Kimball Martin's point that Lean verification does not show the written proof is correct. Wikipedia's Eilenberg–Ganea article (fetched 11 Oct 2026) reports the claim as made on 6 Oct and cites the 23 Sep preprint. The AI attribution is not in the manuscript: the README, preamble and introduction name no model and no human role; the attribution rests on repository-wide sentences ('produced by an internal OpenAI model'; 'The vast majority of results were obtained with the same procedure using an unreleased internal OpenAI model'; about three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute per result on average), and on the manuscript not being among the exceptions the README lists (the list uses 'include'). Earlier, two human-authored preprints claim Whitehead's asphericity question is answered positively. Kawauchi (arXiv:2303.04368, March 2023; v2 April 2024) claims Theorem 1.1, 'Whitehead Aspherical Conjecture is true', without mentioning Eilenberg–Ganea. Pasku (arXiv:2107.12293, July 2021; v2 5 Oct 2026) states that Eilenberg–Ganea is false as 'an immediate implication of our result and that of Bestvina-Brady'. Under the Bestvina–Brady dichotomy, a true Whitehead conjecture forces the bullet to fail, so if either is right the bullet already had a negative answer from 2021 or 2023. I record these as events, not as resolutions: the papers are about Whitehead's question, the bullet's consequence comes only through the dichotomy, neither paper has been published or engaged with in any source I found, and Wikipedia's Whitehead article (Oct 2026) lists Whitehead as unsolved and mentions neither. Pasku's stated theorem covers only the trivial-group, one-relation case; the link to the general question (Howie 1983, Luft 1996 in search summaries) is unverified. Pasku's earlier arXiv:1407.6283 (2014–2019) is a characterization with two versions marked withdrawn without notice text. The OpenAI group is a Bestvina–Brady-type kernel, the family Davis and Leary–Petrosyan named as the more plausible candidate; the two lines of claims are mutually consistent under the dichotomy. Partial, conditional and family-version results are recorded as discounted events: Martínez-Pedroza & Sánchez Saldaña (2021, conditional on a finitely presented counterexample), Leary & Petrosyan (May 2026, conditional transfer from [W_L,W_L] to B_L), Brady–Leary–Nucinkis (2001), Fluch–Leary (2012) and Sánchez Saldaña (2019) for families and Bredon versions, and Gersten (2015) for criteria. Background is Eilenberg–Ganea 1957 (cd ≥ 3 settled) and Bestvina–Brady 1997 (the dichotomy). The Lusternik–Schnirelmann 'Ganea conjecture' is a different problem, disproved by Iwase (1998), and is not counted. A Wall D(2) counterexample from OpenAI (6 Oct 2026, README only read) is recorded as a neighbouring problem. A zeropoint.sh post titled 'Definitive Resolution ... via Twisted Bredon Cohomology' with 'grok-4' in its URL could not be opened, has no date, and is recorded as an unverified claim. The DeepMind formal-conjectures issue (20 Jan 2026) is a formal statement with 'Created by AI, reviewed by me' and no system named, so it is not progress. On dating: the rule is the first public written argument, which is the 6 Oct 2026 public commit, not the authors' 23 Sep date; both are recorded.
competing_reading: Read as 'claimed but not established': no qualified mathematician has publicly checked the argument; the Lean check is OpenAI's own Comparator pipeline with no build log, against definitions in OpenAI's own library rather than Mathlib, so it shows only that the proof matches the statement as written there; the certificate tables are very large and their checking is unknown; the same release withdrew three manuscripts on 7 Oct 2026 for a sign error; and the manuscript's AI attribution rests on repository-wide sentences. On that reading the judging pass should count the 6 Oct 2026 event as an unverified claim and should not treat the bullet as settled. Read as 'settled in the negative by an AI system': the statement is formally checked in a sorry-free solution module; the group is a Bestvina–Brady kernel of the kind the experts already regarded as the more plausible candidate; and the result has the proof structure (cd 2, a three-dimensional model, a homological obstruction) that a counterexample needs. On that reading the bullet is refuted in October 2026 and the AI involvement is substantive. Separately, if the Kawauchi (2023) or Pasku (2021) Whitehead claims were correct, the bullet would have been refuted earlier, by humans, and the judging pass would need to decide which event the status rests on. Both Pasku and Kawauchi are unverified, so I think the earlier dates should not be used without a check.
what_would_settle_it: (1) An independent build of lean/ComparatorChallenges/EilenbergGanea.lean against the solution module under Comparator, with the full transitive import closure reported and every sorry and axiom listed, and an audit of the repository's definitions of cohomologicalDimension, HasClassifyingSpace and the CW-complex library against the standard notions. (2) An expert reading of the paper's argument (the presentation-based obstruction, the localized degree argument and the transport construction) by a group theorist in the area, or its publication, or a specific error identified in it. (3) For the date: the full commit history of preprints/A-finitely-generated-…-2026 and the text of OpenAI's 6 Oct post (not reachable: HTTP 403). (4) For Pasku 2021: the reduction from the trivial-group one-relation case to Whitehead's general question, and the v1–v2 changes; for Kawauchi 2023: a referee or expert account of the reductions Conjecture 1 → 2 → 3. (5) For the zeropoint.sh claim: the post itself, its date and its author. (6) For the Brady–Leary–Nucinkis and Bestvina–Brady dates: the papers themselves.
